title: I.C.E. I.C.E. Baby
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: A proposal to rebrand short-cycle formative assessment using the acronym I.C.E. (Instruct, Check, Evaluate), drawing parallels to ice therapy in sports. The post advocates for educators to implement this framework repeatedly throughout lessons, applying it as frequently as ice is applied to an injury.
points: Short-cycle formative assessment is essential for responsive teaching, but existing acronyms have baggage or cognitive load issues.
The I.C.E. framework (Instruct, Check, Evaluate) must be repeated multiple times per lesson, mirroring how athletes repeatedly ice injuries.
The metaphor works on multiple levels: ice is applied repeatedly in sports, and assessment must happen repeatedly throughout teaching.
Marketing and branding matter in education; simple frameworks help staff adoption and normalize effective teaching practices.
When teachers repeatedly apply I.C.E., results improve—making explicit teaching 'cool' through consistent, responsive instruction cycles.
quotes: Teachers of explicit instruction are relative professionals when it comes to short cycle formative assessment. Teaching as a profession is also obsessed with an acronym, potentially to our own detriment.

When it comes to checking for understanding and responsive teaching there are a few great explanations of what teachers should do and how they should do it. Bronwyn Ryrie-Jones talks about her process of 'Teach/Track/Respond'.
I've always loved sales and marketing. I'm obsessed with branding and the way we make concepts even the theoretical seem exciting and attractive.

If you are injured in a sport, you rarely just ice the injury once. You do it repeatedly until the swelling subsides. When we assess in a short cycle we never do it once in a lesson, we do it repeatedly.
